facts.claim: Byte-Pair Encoding starts from individual characters (or bytes) and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair, learned once during training. At inference, a new prompt is encoded by applying those same learned merges to its characters until no more apply.
facts.source: Sennrich, Haddow & Birch, "Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units" (2015), https://arxiv.org/abs/1508.07909; Hugging Face LLM Course, "Byte-Pair Encoding tokenization", https://huggingface.co/learn/llm-course/chapter6/5

facts.claim: GPT-2 introduced byte-level BPE — the base vocabulary is built from raw bytes (256 symbols), not Unicode characters, so any text can be tokenized without an unknown-token fallback. Every major LLM tokenizer since descends from this approach.
facts.source: Learn Code Camp, "Byte Pair Encoding (BPE): the tokenizer that made GPTs practical", https://learncodecamp.net/bpe/

facts.claim: OpenAI's GPT-4 tokenizer (cl100k_base) has roughly 100,000 tokens; GPT-4o's tokenizer (o200k_base) doubled that to about 200,000 tokens, both built once via BPE merges over huge training corpora.
facts.source: Grokipedia, "O200k_base tokenizer"; Modal Blog, "What is o200k Harmony?", https://modal.com/blog/what-is-o200k-harmony
